But a prescription is increasing from $11 to $200 a month
 Vawn Himmelsbach Thu, October 29, 2026 at 7:00 AM EDT 5 min read Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Retirees will see a monthly bump of 3.6% on their Social Security retirement check starting in January, thanks to the annual cost-of-living (COLA) adjustment. On average, that translates to an extra $75 per month — the biggest bump in four years. 
 While that's in line with inflation, will an extra $75 a month make a significant difference, especially for older Americans facing rising healthcare costs?

 Lorrie Ufkin, 71, told The Associated Press that the COLA increase "doesn't even meet what they're going to do for changes to Medicare ." 
 A temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program helped Americans like Ufkin offset their premiums over the past two years. But the Trump administration is ending that program early, wrapping it up by the end of the year. 
 For Ufkin, that's "catastrophic." Both she and her husband rely on a prescription that will jump from $11 per month to $200 per month. Combined, their monthly out-of-pocket costs will surge from $22 to $400 — completely swallowing their COLA increase. 
 Along with the rising cost of living — everything from gas to groceries to utilities — upcoming healthcare adjustments could deliver a serious blow to your bottom line. 
 Upcoming changes to Part D premiums 
 Open enrollment for Medicare has already begun and runs until Dec. 7. During this window, you can review and update your health and prescription drug coverage. Changes will go into effect Jan. 1, 2027. 
 You can enroll in a standalone prescription drug plan (PDP) through Medicare Part D to supplement your traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage plan. Private insurance companies provide Part D plans with federal approval. 
 But a few major policy shifts could impact your choices for 2027: 
 Ending subsidies: The federal Part D premium subsidies are expiring. 
 Higher out-of-pocket caps: Prices are going to be higher for Medicare Part D drugs, increasing from $2,100 in 2026 to $2,400 in 2027 
 Higher deductibles: The standard deductible is increasing from $615 to $700. 
 The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) says the average standalone Part D premiums will rise by less than $1 per month in 2027. The agency also estimates average Medicare Advantage premiums will fall more than 16%, while overall prescription drug premiums will drop 38%. 
 Story Continues In part, that could be attributed to Medicare-negotiated prices for 15 drugs, which include weight-loss and diabetes medications. 
 But an independent analysis of CMS data by KFF, a nonprofit healthcare research organization, uncovered a more complicated issue. While many enrollees will see only modest premium changes, others face " substantially higher premiums " if they don't switch plans. Enrollees also face a declining selection of standalone Plan D options. 
 Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of KFF's Medicare policy program, wrote on X that raw CMS data fails to deliver. 
 "The data released today don't tell us anything about plan changes underneath the hood to control costs," she wrote . "Are plans dropping drugs from formularies, increasing copays, moving to coinsurance, etc. These features affect patient cost and access as much as (if not more than) premiums." 
 Those changes to the fine print can "affect patient cost and access as much as (if not more than) premiums," she added. 
 Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it's raising alarm bells for older investors 
 What you can do about it 
 If you're facing higher healthcare costs this year, shopping around is necessary so your costs don't skyrocket. 
 AARP, an advocacy group for older Americans, is urging Medicare recipients to carefully review their coverage options before the open enrollment period. 
 "It's more important than ever to shop around , compare your options, and choose the coverage that's best for you," said Nancy LeaMond, AARP's executive vice-president and chief advocacy officer. 
 Here are some steps to take before Dec. 7: 
 Use Medicare Plan Finder: Search and compare current plans at Medicare.gov . 
 Review the formulary: Check whether your current prescription drugs stay on your plan's covered list (formulary) and whether their tier placement, copays or coinsurance rates changed. 
 Watch for restrictions: Look out for new red tape on utilization management, like requiring prior authorization from your doctor for routine medications. 
 Explore options: If you have limited income, apply for the federal Extra Help program, which assists with copays, deductibles and premiums. 
 "Medicare beneficiaries may want to evaluate what other features of their Part D plan might be changing, including what drugs are and aren't covered on the plan's formulary, tier placement of covered drugs, deductibles, and cost-sharing requirements," according to the KFF analysis.
